nameStory: The tricolored bat gets its name from the unique banding pattern on each hair of its back fur. If you could pluck a single hair and examine it closely under a magnifying glass, you'd see three distinct color bands running along its length. This three-toned hair pattern creates a subtle but distinctive appearance that helped scientists give this tiny bat its colorful common name.
description: The tricolored bat is the smallest bat in eastern North America, weighing less than a quarter of an ounce - about the same as a penny! This tiny flier has yellowish-brown fur with that characteristic three-banded hair pattern that gives it its name. Despite its small size, it's a skilled night hunter that catches insects on the wing using echolocation, and it can live nearly fifteen years in the wild.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Incredibly tiny - the smallest bat in eastern North America, weighing only about as much as a penny or two. Body is just 3-4 inches long with a wingspan of 8-10 inches.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to reddish-brown fur that looks almost golden in sunlight. Each individual hair has three color bands - dark at the base, light in the middle, and dark at the tip, creating a subtle tricolored effect.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Flies with a slow, erratic, almost fluttery pattern compared to other bats. Often seen foraging around water sources and forest edges just after sunset.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Roosts in tree foliage and hanging lichens rather than buildings or caves during summer. Look for them in wooded areas near water sources where insects are abundant.

habitat: Found in forested areas throughout New England, especially near streams, ponds, and wetlands where insects are plentiful. During summer, they roost in the foliage of deciduous trees and in beard lichens hanging from branches. They prefer areas with a mix of open water for drinking and foraging, plus dense forest cover for roosting sites.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from hibernation in late spring. Females become pregnant after storing sperm all winter, and you might spot them foraging more actively as they need extra energy.
seasonality.summer: Most active season for observation. Females form small roosting groups in tree foliage while males roost alone. Best time to see their characteristic slow, erratic flight patterns at dusk.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs before hibernation. They begin seeking out hibernation sites and may be seen flying during warm autumn evenings.
seasonality.winter: Hibernates in caves, mines, and other protected areas. Rarely observed during this season as they remain dormant in their winter roosts.

funFact: Female tricolored bats are masters of family planning - they mate in fall but don't actually become pregnant until spring, storing the sperm in their bodies all winter long while they hibernate!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small brown bats, but the tricolored bat's tiny size is the giveaway - if you're looking at the smallest bat you've ever seen, it's probably this one. Its slow, fluttery flight style also distinguishes it from the faster, more direct flight of other small bats.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly called the "eastern pipistrelle" based on the mistaken belief it was related to European pipistrelle bats. Scientists later discovered its closest relative is actually the canyon bat of western North America, leading to the name change to tricolored bat.
compareHints: The tricolored bat is the only member of its genus in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other small bats in the evening bat family, it's distinguished by being significantly smaller and having that distinctive tricolored hair pattern. While other small brown bats might look similar from a distance, none combine the tiny size with the golden-brown coloration and slow flight pattern of the tricolored bat.
